http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/secon.text: A second attack in less than a month struck a liquefied natural gas tanker loaded in Qatar in the Strait of Hormuz, as QatarEnergy's force majeure deliveries have extended further and insurance premiums have climbed.The UK Maritime Trade Operations reported that an unidentified vessel had been struck by a projectile off the coast of Oman. Security consultancies Vanguard Tech and Marisks identified the vessel as the GasLog Shanghai.GasLog confirmed the incident occurred last Friday while the vessel was leaving the strait, and said all crew were safe and accounted for and that the tanker remained stable.The GasLog Shanghai loaded its cargo in Qatar around last Monday and stopped transmitting its position near the strait's western entrance last Friday.It remains unclear who owned the LNG on board. QatarEnergy did not immediately respond to questions about the cargo or whether the incident had affected shipments.GasLog is a Monaco-based LNG shipping company that manages vessels for QatarEnergy and other major gas producers.Significant setbackHormuz is Qatar's only maritime route to international LNG markets. Qatar is the world's second-largest LNG exporter after Australia, shipping approximately 77 million tonnes a year. Almost all of it transits the Strait of Hormuz.The Al Rekayyat, a Qatari-owned tanker carrying LNG, was struck near the strait on 7 July, prompting a three-week pause in Qatari LNG shipments through the waterway.Jean-Christian Heintz, managing director of Switzerland-based LNG consultancy Wideangle LNG, said the second incident was a significant setback."This is a blow to Qatar's perseverance in mitigating the effects of the crisis," Heintz told Euronews.He said QatarEnergy faced the same risk whether it used its own fleet or third-party carriers. "Even though QatarEnergy has the choice between using ships from its own fleet or from third parties, the risk assessment might not differ," Heintz explained.The GasLog Shanghai incident also came days after a drone struck the Energos Winter at Egypt’s Damietta port, causing a fire that spread to another GasLog-managed vessel, the GasLog Salem. No party has claimed responsibility for the Damietta attack.Force majeure remains in placeQatarEnergy has been operating under force majeure on some contracts since March, when Iranian attacks on the Ras Laffan industrial complex and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted production and shipping.The Ras Laffan complex, which QatarEnergy describes as the world's largest LNG production facility, accounts for the bulk of Qatar's export capacity. Two of its production trains were damaged in the March strikes.Italian utility Edison said QatarEnergy had informed it that a further three LNG cargoes would not be delivered, extending force majeure on supplies to the company through the end of September.In total, 24 cargoes scheduled for delivery to Edison between April and the end of September — representing approximately 3 billion cubic metres of natural gas — are now subject to force majeure.Edison said it had replaced 17 of the affected cargoes and remained able to meet its commitments to customers. The utility has a 25-year supply agreement with QatarEnergy, signed in 2009, covering 6.4 billion cubic metres per year.Heintz said he saw little reason for QatarEnergy to lift force majeure while the security situation remained unresolved.He said each new incident was pushing shipowners, cargo traders and insurers to reassess the cost of transiting the Strait of Hormuz. "Insurance premiums, both for ships and the cargoes they carry, can only rise from this point," he explained.Global gas markets had already adjusted significantly to the disruption but the latest incidents combined with strong European demand to refill storage ahead of winter were "certainly bullish for prices," Heintz concluded.

Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images West Bank Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.33 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupied West Bank . The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer. The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said. Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted. View image in fullscreen Mourners at the funeral ceremony of Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images Al-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both had died before they made it to hospital. A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods. When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.” Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler. View image in fullscreen Mourners at the funeral ceremony of Abu Alia and al-Nassan in al-Mughayyir. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Israeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year. The other victims were a 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football team shot in June, a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gate in April, and another 14-year-old killed outside the village mosque in January. “We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April. “This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound. They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks. View image in fullscreen Funeral attenders look out from their village of al-Mughayyir at an Israeli hilltop settlement. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP Since late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outposts surround it in all directions . In late August soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening. At least eight families have fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said. The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday. View image in fullscreen Israeli troops raiding al-Mughayyir in July after settler attacks. Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/Reuters In the south Hebron hills Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children. Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement. It is the 66th Palestinian community that has been wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children. “Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” said Yuli Novak , the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.” A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency which manages civilian affairs in occupied Palestine , said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone. In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, as Firing Zone 918 . It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions. As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the most notoriously violent Israeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA Immigration and asylum UK-France ‘one in one out’ deal to expire on Thursday, say sources Deal aimed at deterring small boat arrivals set to end as talks stall over French demand for EU-wide scheme UK politics live – latest updates Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.09 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 07.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK government’s “one in one out” deal with France , which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said. It is understood that negotiations have stalled over French demands for a Europe-wide deal instead, and a reluctance to scale up the numbers of people exchanged between the two countries. Flights that remove people who have been already detained under the scheme will continue, but they are expected to end within weeks. A UK government source confirmed that the expectation was that the deal would be formally drawn to a close on Thursday. “We would like to see the deal continue. But it’s not the end of the world if it doesn’t because it never got to the scale where it would have been a proper deterrent to people coming to the UK in small boats,” the source said. Negotiations in Paris over how best to tie up the deal are continuing between Home Office staff and their French counterparts. More than 1,400 people who have arrived in the UK via small boats have been sent back to France under the deal, while a reciprocal number of asylum seekers with links to the UK have been flown to the UK from France. The deal had been set to expire in April but was extended to 1 October to help counter the anticipated increase in attempted crossings during the summer. The scheme was announced by Keir Starmer and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in July 2025, with the first flights taking off in September of that year. France has insisted it was a time-limited pilot. But ministers wanted to increase the numbers removed as a deterrent to crossings. In June, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, lauded the scheme as a potential deterrent but still said France was not prepared to go it alone with Britain. “According to information from the UN high commissioner for refugees, word of the scheme is beginning to spread, which is prompting a number of migrants to abandon their plans to make the crossing,” Nuñez told a parliamentary commission. “The value of this scheme is therefore clear. Nevertheless, we consider that France should not bear the burden alone and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the EU and the UK. “I have therefore already made it clear to my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be extended beyond 1 October 2026.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, disclosed to MPs earlier this month that the deal cost about £56,000 for every person sent back to France. She dismissed suggestions that an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis. She said: “It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away, because I promise you it would not,” she said. She said the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns and it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space. “It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said. Between January and 27 September, a total of 19,135 people crossed the Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. https://www.foxnews.com/world/supersonic.text: Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland, marking a major milestone in Nordic defense cooperation amid heightened tensions with Moscow. The mission also came one day before Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed European warnings about the threat from Moscow in the region and mocked Estonia's new defense minister over the Baltic state's preparations for a potential Russian attack. Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens were scrambled after Russian aircraft were detected in the international airspace, according to the Swedish Armed Forces. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS The Russian formation included a Tu-134 transport plane, a high-altitude, supersonic MiG-31 interceptors designed to detect and engage long-range threats; and Su-30 multirole fighter jets which are designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat. "This is what close cooperation looks like in practice," Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman, commander of the Swedish Air Force, said in a statement following the joint operation. "Built over years on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together — as air forces, as nations and as Allies." Concern over Russian military activity along NATO’s eastern flank has grown following a string of airspace violations. These include Russian drones entering Polish airspace, a Mi-8 helicopter crossing from Kaliningrad into Poland, drones crashing in Romania and Moldova, and armed Russian jets entering Estonian airspace before being intercepted by NATO aircraft on Sept. 18. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT In Estonia, Defense Minister Martin Herem warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia within a year and argued that Tallinn must determine whether its defenses are sufficient for such a scenario. Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the government is ready to shut down border crossing points on short notice if threat assessments change, according to reports. Speaking at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum on Friday, Putin pushed back against such warnings. "Many people in Europe say they expect an attack from Russia and therefore claim they must prepare for war with Russia," Putin said. "I want to emphasize once again: we are not preparing for military action against Europe. We have no such plans, no basis for them, and, most importantly, no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe." Putin then mocked Herem's warnings: "As we jokingly say in Russia: 'The circus has left, but the clowns remain.' It is political clowning. ... Clearly, these statements are complete nonsense and absurdity," Putin said, according to EurAsia Daily. FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE Estonia sits across the Gulf of Finland from Finland, with the three countries forming part of NATO's increasingly integrated northern and eastern defenses amid concerns about Russian military activity. Finland formally joined NATO as its 31st member in April 2023, roughly doubling the alliance's land border with Russia. Sweden followed as the 32nd member in March 2024. Estonia, which regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has been a NATO member since 2004. The Baltic Sea region has also remained on heightened alert following incidents involving gas pipelines, sabotage and hybrid threats since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters has reported. NATO said in June that it was enhancing protection of its eastern members in the cyber and space domains while helping countries build resilience against what it describes as hostile Russian actions, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations. NATO says its military activities along the eastern flank are entirely defensive and that it is "ready, willing and able to defend every Ally." FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS The alliance has said an attack against any member would be met with a "resounding response." NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently underscored Washington's role in the alliance during a visit to Iowa, telling The Associated Press that Putin "knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined." "We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it," Rutte said. "And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough," he warned. European intelligence officials said Sept. 24 that Russia could test NATO's defenses. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service assessed the risk of a limited Russian military attack against a NATO country in the coming months as "low but growing" and said Moscow is expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West.
